output:
Start the payment move only after two things happen: the service owner signs the release ticket, and the operations lead confirms the rollback snapshot works. Do not start if either check is missing. Before touching any traffic, the release engineer must write down the start time, the current error rate, and the database replication delay.

Stage 1: send 10% of traffic to the new service for 30 minutes. Keep eyes on payment failures, double charges, p95 latency, and replication delay. Hard rule: even one double charge stops everything right away. If payment failures go over 0.5% for five minutes in a row, send 100% of traffic back to the old service. If p95 latency stays above 800 ms for ten minutes, stop and ask the service owner if you should keep going. These numbers are strict rules, not loose ideas.

Keep tracking these exact same numbers during the whole move. You must track them to get proof. Proof tells you what to do. Never move forward just because the clock says it is time. If the 10% stage goes well, move 50% of traffic for 60 minutes and follow the exact same stop rules. Never jump straight to 100%, even if the first stage looks totally fine.

Once you reach 100%, keep the old service ready to take back traffic for seven days. Put the move log at /var/log/payments/migration.json and put its checksum on ticket PAY-2048. You must run `payments verify --ticket PAY-2048` and see it pass before turning off the old service. Tell the customer support team before you make any traffic change, and keep all old logs until the incident review period is over.
